body_markdown:
Weight loss injections such as Wegovy and Mounjaro have become increasingly popular among people looking to manage obesity and, in some cases, type 2 diabetes. However, new UK research has raised questions about how these medicines could affect patients undergoing surgery and anaesthesia.


A study involving tens of thousands of surgical patients found that people using GLP-1 medicines had a higher rate of regurgitation or pulmonary aspiration during procedures compared with those who were not taking these medicines.


The researchers reported an approximately 11-fold higher incidence of these complications among GLP-1 users. However, importantly, the study did not establish that the medicines directly caused the increased risk.


## What are GLP-1 weight loss injections?


GLP-1 medicines are a group of treatments used for conditions including obesity and type 2 diabetes. Popular medicines in this category include semaglutide, found in Wegovy and Ozempic, and tirzepatide, the active ingredient in Mounjaro.


These medicines can influence appetite and digestion. One of their effects is to slow the rate at which food and fluids leave the stomach.


This effect can be useful as part of weight management because it can contribute to feelings of fullness. However, it may also be relevant when a person needs an operation involving general anaesthesia.


## Why could stomach emptying matter during surgery?


Patients preparing for surgery are normally given instructions about when they should stop eating and drinking before an operation.


These fasting periods are intended to reduce the amount of material in the stomach while the patient is under anaesthesia. This matters because stomach contents can sometimes move back towards the throat, a process known as regurgitation.


If stomach contents enter the lungs, it is known as pulmonary aspiration. This can potentially block the airway or lead to lung infections and other serious complications.


Because GLP-1 medicines can slow gastric emptying, researchers have been investigating whether people taking these medicines could have a greater amount of food or fluid remaining in their stomach during anaesthesia.


## What did the UK study find?


Researchers from Guy's and St Thomas' NHS Foundation Trust and King's College London studied adults undergoing elective or emergency procedures that required anaesthesia.


The researchers examined data from 47,039 patients across 119 sites in the UK.


Among these patients, 1,348 people, equivalent to 2.9 percent, reported using weight loss injections during the three months before their operation.


Almost 70 percent of these patients were taking tirzepatide, the active ingredient in Mounjaro. A further 26.2 percent were taking semaglutide, which is found in medicines including Wegovy and Ozempic.


The researchers also identified 20 patients who reported taking daily weight loss pills.


## How common were the complications?


Among the 45,691 patients who were not using weight loss medicines, 57 experienced regurgitation or aspiration. This represented approximately one case for every 802 patients.


Among the 1,348 people using GLP-1 medicines, 19 experienced one of the complications. This represented approximately one case for every 71 patients.


The researchers therefore reported that the rate of regurgitation and aspiration was around 11 times higher among GLP-1 users.


Of the 19 GLP-1 users who experienced complications, 17 had regurgitation and two experienced pulmonary aspiration. The study reported that regurgitation most commonly occurred while patients were emerging from anaesthesia.


## Does this prove weight loss injections cause surgical complications?


No. This is an important distinction when interpreting the findings.


The researchers themselves stated that the study could identify an association but could not determine causality. In other words, the results show that GLP-1 medicine use and these complications occurred together more frequently, but they do not establish that the medication itself was responsible for every case.


There are also other factors that can influence the risk of pulmonary aspiration.


For example, obesity and diabetes are recognised risk factors for aspiration. These conditions are also more common among people receiving GLP-1 medicines.


This means other differences between the groups could have contributed to the findings.


## What did the researchers say about stopping treatment?


The study also highlighted differences in how patients managed their GLP-1 medicines before surgery.


According to the research report, fewer than one third of GLP-1 users were asked to stop their treatment before surgery. Those who did stop generally discontinued their medicines or pills for between eight and 14 days.


The researchers noted that this period may not always be sufficient for the medicines to be completely eliminated from the body.


They estimated that between 25 and 35 days could be required for effective elimination of the drugs.


However, decisions about whether a medicine should be stopped before an operation depend on the individual patient, the medication involved and the type of procedure. Patients should not stop prescribed treatment without discussing it with their doctor or surgical team.


## What should patients tell their surgical team?


One of the clearest messages from the research is the importance of telling medical professionals about GLP-1 medicines before surgery.


Patients should inform their surgeon, anaesthetist or other relevant healthcare professional if they are taking medicines such as Wegovy, Mounjaro or Ozempic.


This information can help the medical team assess potential risks and make appropriate decisions about preparation for anaesthesia.


The researchers also advised patients to disclose their use of weight loss injections regardless of where the treatment was obtained.


This may be particularly relevant as some patients in the study obtained their treatments through online pharmacies rather than from a GP or hospital specialist.


## Common side effects of weight loss injections


GLP-1 medicines can cause a range of side effects. Reported effects include nausea, heartburn, vomiting, diarrhoea and constipation.


Some people may also experience headaches or reactions around the injection site, including redness, bruising, itching, swelling or pain.


Gallstones and inflammation of the gallbladder have also been reported.


Side effects can vary from person to person, and patients should follow the advice provided by their healthcare professional and the medicine's prescribing information.


## What does the research mean for people taking GLP-1 medicines?


The findings do not mean that people taking weight loss injections should automatically stop their treatment or avoid surgery.


Instead, the study highlights a potential issue that healthcare teams may need to consider when patients taking GLP-1 medicines undergo anaesthesia.


The research also demonstrates why medication history is an important part of pre-operative assessment. Understanding which medicines a patient takes can help clinicians consider factors that may affect anaesthesia and surgical care.


For anyone scheduled for an operation, the safest approach is to provide the medical team with a complete and accurate list of current medicines and follow their specific instructions about eating, drinking and medication before surgery.


## Final thoughts


Weight loss injections have changed the way obesity and related health conditions can be managed, but research into their effects continues.


The new UK study found an association between GLP-1 medicine use and a higher incidence of regurgitation or pulmonary aspiration during surgery. The reported rate was around 11 times higher among GLP-1 users in the study.


However, the researchers stressed that the findings cannot prove that GLP-1 medicines directly caused these complications. Other factors, including obesity and diabetes, may also contribute to aspiration risk.


For patients preparing for surgery, one practical point stands out: make sure your healthcare team knows about any GLP-1 medicine you are taking. This allows clinicians to consider your individual circumstances and make appropriate decisions about your treatment and anaesthesia.
